Subject: Denis, please stop the sale and call me

Denis,

I am writing in English so there is no misunderstanding, and so you and your wife can both read this. I have tried to write it several times already. I am still very angry, but I want you to read this knowing one thing: I do not want to lose my brother. I do want you to understand how badly you have hurt me, and I need you to stop what is happening with the building.

On Thursday at six in the morning, I was shaping baguettes when a photographer from the agency came into my shop. That is how I learned you were putting the building up for sale. Not from you. From a stranger with a camera, standing in the bakery where I have worked for 31 years.

He told me that Mr. Denis had said I was all right with it.

I had agreed to nothing. I did not even know there was anything to agree to. Karine had to calm me down. Imagine having to stand there in front of your employee and a stranger while you discover that your own brother has made a decision like this without telling you.

Afterward, I found the listing on Centris. Our building, listed at $1,150,000. I had to go online to find out what was happening to a property I own half of, and to the place where I earn my living.

I need you to understand that this was humiliating as well as frightening. That photographer was only doing his job. He should never have been put in the position of telling me something that should have come from you.

After maman’s funeral, you called me and said, “No rush, we decide together.” I remember those words very clearly. Since she died in February, there has been enough to deal with. The estate was settled in August. I believed that whatever came next, we would talk about it together, as you said we would.

Together cannot mean that you arrange a sale from Calgary and I find out when someone arrives to take photographs.

This is not only about my attachment to papa’s building, although I will not pretend that means nothing. He bought it in 1979. The bakery downstairs, the two apartments above, the room in the back where he used to let you sleep among the flour sacks when we were children. You loved that room. You have your own memories of this place. I know you do.

But before you dismiss me as being sentimental, please look at the business that is here now. I have spent 31 years building it. There are six employees whose jobs matter. There are customers who have been coming for years, people who count on us and whom we know by name. There is work here every morning long before most people are awake. This is not a family souvenir I am refusing to let go of. It is a working bakery, and it is my livelihood.

I have paid the rent of $2,400 a month to the estate, never late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 out of my own pocket for the new roof. I mention that because I need you to recognize that I have taken responsibility for this place. I have put money into it, not just feelings.

You may have your own reasons for wanting to sell. You may need the money, or you may simply not want to own a building in Montreal while you live in Calgary. I can understand wanting to discuss that. I cannot understand why you did not call me before putting it on the market.

And I cannot understand what happened to the conversation we had in September.

I told you on the phone that I wanted to buy your half. I told you the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. That was a serious offer to work toward a solution, not something I said in passing. I had gone to the caisse because I wanted to find a way for you to receive your money and for me to keep the bakery here.

I understand that my financing does not automatically settle the value of your share. We might have needed an independent valuation. We might have needed to discuss the difference between what I can borrow and what you expect. Those would not necessarily have been easy conversations, but at least we would have been having them.

Instead, I am looking at a public listing and wondering whether you ever intended to give me a real chance.

My lease ends on April 30, 2027. That is close enough that I cannot treat this sale as something happening far away in the future. I do not know who would buy the building or what they would do. What frightens me is a developer buying it to demolish it or turn it into condos, or a new owner demanding rent I cannot afford. If my rent doubles, the bakery cannot survive it.

I cannot just pick up 31 years of business and move it somewhere else without enormous cost and risk. You need to consider that before treating this as an ordinary property sale.

So here is what I am asking you to do.

Please have the building taken off the market this week while we speak properly and work through the options. At the very least, give me the first opportunity to reach an agreement to buy your half before you move forward with an outside buyer. I mean a genuine opportunity, with the information and time needed to put a purchase together, not a last-minute chance after everything has already been arranged.

Also, please tell the agent that I have not agreed to photographs or visits inside the bakery. No one should be telling people that I have given permission when I have not. Any arrangements involving the shop need to be discussed with me beforehand.

Then call me yourself, this week. I do not want to try to resolve this through text messages, and I do not want an answer passed along by your wife. I have written in English so we can all understand the same letter, but this conversation needs to be between you and me. You are my brother. I need to hear from you directly.

I will listen to what you have to say. I cannot promise I will not be angry on the phone. I am angry, and I am not going to pretend otherwise just to make this easier. But I will listen, and I want you to listen to me too.

What hurts most is that you knew this would affect my whole life, and you let me discover it from someone else. I keep coming back to that. You could have called. Even if you knew the conversation would be difficult, you could have called.

We have already lost papa and maman. I do not want us to lose each other over this building. But keeping our relationship cannot mean that I stay quiet while decisions are made behind my back. I need honesty from you, and I need a say in what happens next.

Please stop the sale process and call me. Let us have the conversation we should have had before that photographer ever walked through my door.
